posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text:
$CBRS — the guide did the heavy lifting.

$CBRS builds wafer-scale AI chips — one giant chip instead of many small ones — and increasingly sells access to them as a cloud service rather than selling the hardware. Customers rent inference capacity, $CBRS keeps the chips and charges for use. That shift is the story: cloud revenue is growing fast while hardware sales shrink.

Today's print split in two. On the headline numbers it missed, with a wider loss. On its own core measure it beat, with core revenue of $230.9M. Then the guide did the work: next quarter is guided at $310–330M of core revenue, well above consensus, against a $26B backlog, and a new agreement with $MSFT was disclosed, size undisclosed. Shares jumped after hours.

The honest distinction: a raised guide and a big backlog prove demand is real. They do not prove profitability is near — the loss widened a lot on the headline numbers, and the gap between the core measure and the headline is wide. The reliability question from the short seller was answered by the CEO weeks ago; what this print tested was whether the economics hold up, and the cloud growth is the evidence for it.

Long term, if the cloud model scales, $CBRS becomes a recurring-revenue inference provider with a cost edge from building at wafer scale. If hardware economics or chip reliability bite, the story is the capex. The print backs the demand side. The cost side is still being proven.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text:
$TE — the miss was demand-side, the question is still financing.

$TE makes solar modules and cells in Texas. It builds the panels and sells them to developers building solar projects. The Dallas plant is ramping, and the Austin cell fab is due to start producing cells early next year — making its own cells instead of importing them. Most of next year's capacity is already contracted.

Today's print missed the revenue bar by nearly 30%. The bigger item is what did not change: the financing for the Austin fab is still not closed. Talks are exclusive and it is the company's number one priority, and the build pace has been slowed to match the financing timeline. Contracted 2027 capacity is over 3.5 GW, lower than the figure carried into the print. Unrestricted cash is $59.5M.

The honest distinction: contracted capacity proves customers want the product. It does not prove the factory gets built on time without the financing package. The tax-credit question is still open, not decided.

Long term, if the cells arrive on time and the financing closes, this is a US manufacturer with contracted demand in a market that needs domestic supply. If either slips, the story stretches. The print resolved neither.

posts.name: InvestmentGuru
posts.text:
$NBIS — the print beat, the funding plan didn't.

$NBIS rents out AI compute. It builds data centers full of GPUs and sells the capacity to customers training and running AI models, on multi-year contracts. The model is contract-first: customers sign long deals and pay upfront, and $NBIS uses that money to build the next data center.

Today's print beat the bar on revenue. The market sold it anyway, because the funding plan is the story now. Next year's build is far bigger than next year's revenue — 2027 revenue is guided at $12–13B against $40–45B of capex — and the $7B annual recurring revenue target slipped a few months. Cash sits at $7.4B.

The honest distinction: contracted revenue proves demand is real. It does not prove the build is funded. The offset is that customers are effectively financing the expansion — prepayments plus contract-backed financing are meant to cover most of next year's build. What that does not prove is that the pace holds if a customer slows down, or if debt markets stay shut to names like this.
Long term, if it executes, the contracted backlog converts into a very large revenue base. The risk is the gap between building now and getting paid later. That gap is the whole thesis now.

posts.name: Dividendology
posts.text:
$MPLX has now increased its quarterly distribution by 12.5% for three consecutive years!

Incredible distribution growth… But even more incredible considering that it’s current yield is 8.2%.

The Chowder Rule adds a stock’s dividend yield to its annual dividend growth rate to assess its combination of income and growth.

Using MPLX’s 8.2% yield and 12.5% distribution growth rate gives it a Chowder score of 20.7, comfortably above the commonly used 12-point target.

This gives them an astounding ‘Chowder Score’ of 20.7-

But understanding the business behind that income is important.

MPLX owns pipelines, storage terminals, natural-gas gathering and processing facilities, and infrastructure that separates natural gas liquids into usable products.

Customers primarily pay fees to move, store, and process energy products.

Long-term agreements with Marathon Petroleum include minimum-volume commitments and payments for reserved capacity-

Which makes cash flows FAR more predictable than those of an oil and gas producer.

Commodity prices still affect production activity and certain processing arrangements, but MPLX’s earnings are less directly dependent on the price of each barrel produced.

For businesses like this, growing distributable cash flow per unit is a primary driver of intrinsic value.

It supports the distributions investors receive, while retained cash can help fund growth and reduce debt.

Distributable cash flows per share is still well covering the distributions-

But keep in mind that between 2023 and 2025, annual distributions increased from approximately $3.25 to $4.07 per unit, roughly 25%.

But distributable cash flow per share increased from approximately $5.23 to $5.68, roughly 9%.

Distributions grew faster than the cash flow supporting them, which does narrow the coverage cushion.

With that being said, they’re still sitting at a distribution coverage ratio of around 1.3x.

The payout remains covered, but maintaining 12.5% annual increases indefinitely would require stronger cash-flow growth.

Moving forward, I would expect lower distribution growth.

More than likely the distribution growth will be in line with EBITDA growth.

And keep in mind that debt has also grown faster than trailing adjusted EBITDA.

MPLX’s leverage ratio increased from 3.1 times at year-end 2024 to 3.8 times in September 2026.

With that being said, the company still has very reasonable debt/leverage ratios.

Now, let’s compare MPLX with other large midstream businesses.

MPLX offers the highest starting yield and fastest recent payout growth in this group.

The valuation snapshot also places it approximately 16% below Kinder Morgan and 32% below Williams on EV/EBITDA.

EPD does trade at a lower multiple with better leverage ratios-

But the yield is lower with much slower distribution growth.

MPLX is attractive for investors seeking High Yield, but don’t expect the same level of distribution growth we’ve seen over the last 3 years.

posts.name: Jason Luongo
posts.text:
You could get paid $1,230 today on 100 shares of $AMD you already own.

It's called a covered call, and here's how it works:

$AMD trades around $582, so 100 shares are worth about $58,200. You sell one $700 call expiring December 18 and collect about $12.30 a share, or $1,230, up front. That strike is about 20% above today's price.

In exchange, you agree to sell your 100 shares at $700 if AMD is above that price on December 18.

At expiration, one of two things happens:

1. $AMD finishes below $700. The call expires worthless. You keep the $1,230 and your shares, a 2.1% return in 36 days, and you're free to sell another call.

2. $AMD finishes above $700. Your shares are sold at $700. That's an $11,805 gain from today's price plus the $1,230 premium, or $13,035 in total (22.4%).

You don't have to wait until expiration either. I usually buy the call back once it has lost about half its value, then sell the next one.

The catch: your upside stops at $700. If $AMD runs to $800, the gains above $700 go to the call buyer. The premium also doesn't protect you much on the way down. It only cushions $12.30 a share, so your breakeven from today's price is $569.65.

$AMD isn't expected to report earnings again until after December 18, so there's no earnings report inside this trade.

Only sell a call at a strike where you'd be happy to sell your shares.

Not financial advice. I share these for education.

posts.text:
Nebius earningscall and the total lack of business development and understanding on X. $NBIS 

First, I saw a lot of comments on X about the quality of the earnings call and the level of excitement. Well, I can kill that immediately, because I found that Arkady sounded very confident and very relaxed on the call.

I liked his comment that demand for AI is real and substantial, and everything else, like building the capacity and financing it, is a task. Tasks can be hard, but they can be solved.

They are seeing customers committing to them for longer, at higher prices, and paying more upfront, as we are seeing across the industry as well.

Q3 agreements closed above $25 million per megawatt, another step up from $20–25 million per megawatt. The agreements are also getting larger. They signed their first billion-dollar-plus contract three months ago, and now they are signing multibillion-dollar agreements for their AI cloud.

And the customer profile, with enterprise leaders like Databricks, Datadog and Snowflake signing multiyear agreements, is also freaking strong.

The strength of Nebius, and what they do smartly, is that they sell across three time horizons. They optimize the mix between the three.

First, spot and short-term contracts at premium prices. Then one-to-three-year contracts, which lock in more revenue visibility. This is the core business, which is logical because it sits between opportunistic and stable.

The third is five-year agreements with investment-grade hyperscalers. Those contracts support debt financing and provide a more stable base for the buildout.

Super logical. We have talked about this many times. It is a really strong business approach that balances financial security with the flexibility to be opportunistic. Strategically excellent.

To build on that, Nebius’s CEO already explained that, on top of prepayments, they raise financing against the investment-grade contracts. Going back to those three business models, that financing allows them to be more opportunistic with spot-market demand.

Like, what’s not logical about this?

As that flywheel grows, they can pursue more spot-market demand, supported by financing backed by that third leg: hyperscalers and other customers on long-term, multiyear contracts.

And to use a quote:

“We invest in three things at once: the capacity, the software platform, and go-to-market that meets customers where they are. All three matter equally, but capacity is the foundation of the business. It defines our scale.”

Totally in line with Nebius strategy thay they have layed out a long while ago. And smarter than the rest, in my opinion.

People are now getting hung up on Nebius stopping ARR guidance, but I think that is completely logical. First of all, I have been vocal about hating that metric from the beginning. I think it is a useless metric, especially when you look at Nebius.

Take those three business models into account. If you build for on-demand capacity, you cannot safely guide for ARR. You do not know what spot pricing will be at the time, and you do not know how much capacity you are going to sell. This is the opportunistic side of the business.

So I have zero problems with stopping ARR guidance, because it does not tell you shit. What matters much more is how much revenue they are going to generate. And yes, you are not going to have full visibility into that, because part of the business is opportunistic.

But smart management is chasing where the money is. And that money is the basis for all the capacity expansions. So yes, I think it is smart.

The Justice Department is investigating whether companies tied to Alice Huang, the woman at the center of the Nvidia scandal, helped smuggle Super Micro $SMCI products into China, per Bloomberg.

The probe is being led by the US attorney’s office in Manhattan. It’s unclear whether it’s connected to existing chip-smuggling cases.

Manhattan prosecutors already charged Super Micro co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and two others in March. They’re accused of conspiring to ship Nvidia-powered servers to a Southeast Asian company and divert them to Chinese customers. Liaw has pleaded not guilty and left the company. Super Micro itself isn’t a defendant and says it’s cooperating.

The DOJ is separately investigating Megaspeed International, Huang’s former company, over suspected chip smuggling. Megaspeed denies wrongdoing.

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE NVIDIA: WHAT PENALTIES, FINANCIAL RESTRICTIONS, AND OTHER CONSEQUENCES THE COMPANY CAN FACE (1/2)

BOTTOM LINE

As of 11/12/26, no penalty, charge, listing, denial order, subpoena, or contract action against NVIDIA itself has been announced by any authority. What exists: a DOJ National Security Division criminal inquiry into Megaspeed (BIS paused its own administrative inquiry at DOJ's request); an FBI look at Huang personally, per President Trump on 11/9; the board's independent investigation (Wachtell Lipton, Joon H. Kim, retained 11/10); the Kistenmacher securities class action filed 11/9; and a House briefing for 11/18 that has been requested, not subpoenaed. The realistic worst case for the company, if a knowing violation is proved, is a nine-figure to low-ten-figure BIS settlement with audits and a suspended denial order, priced off Seagate ($300M, 2023) and Applied Materials ($252M, February 2026, the statutory maximum on its facts). The larger financial risk is not a fine at all: it is licensing restriction and legislation, the functional equivalent of the Wells Fargo asset cap. And one correction to the morning's framing matters: Singapore's own statement, published 11/12, contradicts several circulating claims about Alice Huang, including parts of the circulating account (see Section 5.3).

A framing correction that runs through everything below: modern BIS enforcement runs under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 (ECRA, 50 USC 4819), not IEEPA. The numbers are similar; the authority, and the correct civil maximum, are ECRA's.

THE GATING FACT FOR THE ENTIRE EXPORT CASE

Megaspeed was not on the Entity List, received no BIS is-informed letter according to Nvidia, and Nvidia says it placed Megaspeed on its own internal block list in June 2025. A sale by Nvidia to a non-listed Singapore or Malaysia cloud operator is not, without more, an EAR violation. Company liability requires BIS or DOJ to prove a license requirement was triggered, through knowledge (including reason to know, awareness of a high probability, or willful avoidance, 15 CFR 772.1), a General Prohibition 10 violation, or causing or aiding a violation (15 CFR 764.2(e)-(g)). That proof question, not the penalty arithmetic, is what the DOJ inquiry will decide. The single most damaging reported fact on knowledge: Nvidia's on-site verification covered roughly 86,000 of the roughly 136,000 GPUs Bloomberg's customs analysis shows Megaspeed affiliates importing, leaving a gap of roughly 50,000 units. BIS's July 2024 diversion guidance treats proceeding in the face of unexplained red flags as aggravating.

SECTION 1: EXPORT CONTROL ENFORCEMENT AGAINST NVIDIA ITSELF

1.1 BIS administrative penalties.

Maximum: ECRA authorizes a civil fine of not more than $300,000 or twice the value of the transaction that is the basis of the violation, whichever is greater, per violation. Inflation-adjusted, the current figure is $374,474 per violation or twice transaction value, effective 1/15/25, with no 2026 adjustment (BIS penalties page, read 11/12/26). BIS counts per shipment or transfer: Seagate had 429 occasions; Cadence had 61 violations. Applied to the aggregate of violative transactions, the twice-value prong is how modern settlements are built. Illustrative arithmetic only: twice the $4.6B Bloomberg Megaspeed tally is $9.2B, but that figure is legally articulable only if BIS first proves substantially all of those sales were Nvidia violations, which is the weakest link in the chain given the gating fact above.

Realistic: governed by BIS's September 2024 Administrative Enforcement Guidelines. A voluntary self-disclosure caps the base penalty at half the statutory maximum in egregious cases; deliberate non-disclosure of a significant violation is a formal aggravating factor; non-monetary penalties (audits, training, suspended denial orders) are the stated preference for lesser cases. Nvidia has no reported VSD; its public posture through 10/30

This is crazy 🤯

Someone is willing to pay me about $1,150 to buy $MRVL at $150 by January 15.

It's called a cash-secured put, and here's how it works:

Marvell trades around $166. You sell one $150 put expiring January 15 and collect about $11.50 a share, or $1,150, up front. You set aside $15,000 in cash in case you have to buy 100 shares at $150.

At expiration, one of two things happens:

1. Marvell is above $150. The put expires worthless and you keep the full $1,150, a 7.7% return on your cash in about 9 weeks.

2. Marvell is below $150. You buy 100 shares at $150, but since you already collected $11.50, your real cost is $138.50 a share, about 16% below today's price.

The premium is this high because Marvell is volatile right now. The stock sold off hard on its all-stock deal to buy Lumentum (first reported Oct 29, announced Nov 2), and the options are pricing in about 71% implied volatility.

The risk: Marvell reports earnings on December 1, before this put expires. If it finishes below $138.50, you're holding shares at a loss. Only sell puts on stocks you'd be happy to own at the strike.

I'm slightly disappointed in the $NBIS Q3 results and Q4 guidance but the stock doesn't deserve to be down -16% today, I believe this is just investors overreacting to a couple short term hiccups... 

Q3 revs up +571% YoY
Q3 revs up +68% QoQ
Q3 ebitda of $465M, up from -$5M a year ago
Q3 ebitda margins were 47%

Here are some of the reasons why the market might be overreacting today: 

1) Q4 revs and 2026 exit ARR will be lighter than expected because of construction / power delays, pushing those revenues into early 2027. 
~These revenues didn't disappear, they just got pushed back a few months... looks bad but doesn't change long term thesis/opportunity. This just proves how hard it is to build these large data centers with so many potential delays across construction, power, and permits. 

2) 2027 revenue guidance starts at $12-13B, perhaps a little lower than some were expecting
~Management said this is very conservative guidance and I believe they need to start low in case they run into additional construction delays next year. I believe there's meaningful upside to this range if schedules in 2027 stay on track and $NBIS is able to deliver capacity on-time to customers. 

3) 2027 capex guide of $40-45B 
~This capex guide looks big compared to the $12-13B revenue guide which is why I think it's a mistake for $NBIS management to stop giving ARR guidance. ARR guidance gives us an idea of the capacity ramp throughout the year and helps us model out when power gets connected and when revenues start to get collected. There's going to be a disconnect between revenues and ARR... especially in a business like this where capacity is ramping fast but those revenues don't come for a few months after the power gets connected.

Look at Anthropic... they're expected to do $50-52B revenues in 2026 however their exit ARR is expected to be ~$100B. I think it will be similar for $NBIS although perhaps even more dramatic based on when their 1GW of capacity gets connected in 2027. I think it's very likely that $NBIS does $15-16B revs in 2027 but their exit ARR is $30-32B 

Here are my 2027 exit ARR predictions that I shared yesterday... https://x.com/JonahLupton/status/2120574426479788167?a=QuoKWBWJDBF6IMfKBmI&s=20

I'm sticking with these ARR predictions because management has confirmed they expect to add another 1GW of capacity in CY2027 which should generate ~$25B of ARR across short, medium, long term deals/pricing. The long term deals are with the hyperscalers at $12-13M per MW. The medium term deals are 1-3 years at $20-35M per MW. The short term deals are under 1 year and could be $35-50M per MW. 

That $40-45B capex number should not surprise anyone because we've known for months that it costs $40-50B to bring on 1GW of capacity -- Jensen and multiple CEO have said this. It's just the capex vs 2027 revenue guidance is scaring some investors and it shouldn't because ARR is the more important number to model with and exit ARR in 2027 will be ~2x higher than the CY2027 revenue number 

Okay, now to the more positive nuggets from the call because there were lots of them...
1) demand is still extremely high, 2027 is basically sold out and starting to sell capacity for 2028
2) will keep adding 1GW per year... still targeting 5GW of connected/contracted power 
3) asset light business model is starting to generate meaningful revenues 
4) prepayments are getting bigger... covering 50-100% of capex with access to asset backed loans when needed
5) payback periods keep getting shorter... coming into 2026 they were 24+ months... with Q2 earnings they said it was down to 22 months and now the payback period is down to 19 months... I suspect this number keeps going lower as MW prices keep going higher while shifting more capacity to short term deals at higher rates. 
6) continue to sign more medium term deals (1-3 years) at above $25M per MW 

I'm going to read through the transcript in a little bit to make sure I didn't miss anything. Wiil add more

I’ve received a couple of questions today on $IREN:

1. How do I think $IREN will be affected by $NVDA, the preferred status and the $70 buy option?

2. How likely is IREN to get acquired in the coming years?

I’ll answer both here:

1/ I actually see the NVIDIA relationship as a major positive for IREN.

Preferred Partner status gives IREN credibility, access to NVIDIA’s ecosystem and potentially a competitive advantage when deploying infrastructure.

But it’s important to understand that it’s not a guaranteed $70 floor. NVIDIA has the right to purchase up to 30M shares over five years, subject to conditions and GPU delivery milestones. That’s potentially $2.1B of investment.

Obviously, NVIDIA has its own problems right now, but I don’t think IREN’s investment thesis should depend on Jensen Huang or NVIDIA’s stock performance.

What matters is whether demand for AI infrastructure continues and whether IREN can execute.

I see NVIDIA as a strategic partner, and not the entire investment thesis.

2/ Acquisition… Honestly, I think it’s possible, but I wouldn’t put a high probability on it.

IREN has something that’s INCREDIBLE difficult to replicate: power, land, data center infrastructure and the ability to deploy GPUs at scale.

That makes them strategically interesting to hyperscalers and other major technology companies.

But I also think IREN has ambitions to become a major AI cloud provider in its own right. With the current growth opportunities, I don’t see management necessarily wanting to sell.

Furthermore the board has made a pretty substantial commitment to keeping the founders around through 2033.

My base case is that IREN continues building independently.

For full transparency. I have shares in $IREN, so I could obviously be biased here.

-BP

$VLO $MPC $PSX $DK $CLMT WHAT CITGO'S RECORD QUARTER MEANS FOR VALERO, MARATHON, PHILLIPS 66, AND DELEK

Citgo is confirmation for Q3 and a direction signal for Q4. It does not change any listed refiner's story; it tells you where in the stack each name sits as cracks roll over.

WHAT CITGO ACTUALLY PROVES

Citgo is the cleanest capture read in the complex: no midstream, no chemicals, no retail network of scale, just three refineries run at 103% of rated capacity into the distillate spike, with a record 365,000 bpd of distillate production (about 40% of total input, a very distillate-heavy yield for a US system). Its refining EBITDA works out to about $38 per barrel of total throughput for the quarter ($3,162M of refining EBITDA on 904,000 bpd over 92 days), or about $40 per barrel on crude runs alone (855,000 bpd). In Q2 the same math gave about $18 per barrel. Citgo's realized capture roughly doubled in one quarter, in line with the crack.

That sits right on top of what the listed names already printed for Q3. Valero, the first and cleanest print of the season, posted a record quarter: adjusted EPS $23.90 against roughly $21.1 of consensus, refining operating income of $8.8B against $1.6B a year ago, and a realized refining margin of $39.24/bbl against $13.14 a year ago, a 97.8% capture rate against its own $40.14/bbl Gulf Coast 3-2-1 benchmark (93.5% in the Gulf Coast region alone). Phillips 66 realized $38.00/bbl on its worldwide realized margin line, at the low bound of its expected range. So the Q3 capture environment was real and industry-wide at the Gulf Coast complexes, not a Valero accounting artifact.

Two control cases keep the claim honest. PBF, weighted to the East and West Coasts and the Midcontinent rather than the Gulf Coast export complex, realized $34.56/bbl and scored below its expected range: capture was a Gulf Coast distillate story, not a rising tide. And Marathon's $45.70/bbl refining and marketing margin is a different, definitional line (it carries purchased product and marketing economics), it came in well below its own expected range, and the definitional premium it normally carries over the benchmark compressed sharply versus Q2. Citgo does not rehabilitate that, because Citgo has almost no marketing book to dilute or inflate the line.

THE FORWARD SIGNAL IS THE GUIDE CUT, AND IT APPLIES TO ALL FOUR

Citgo guided Q4 implied EBITDA of $2.44B to $2.74B, down from October's implied $2.94B to $3.24B, explicitly on early-November forward curves. Annualized that is still roughly $10B, so Q4 is a step down from a peak, not a normalization to normal. Every listed refiner's Q4 consensus was marked on roughly the same curve window, so the read-across is: Q4 refining earnings come in down quarter over quarter for all four names, but at levels still several times mid-cycle.

The latest EIA weekly release is the first hard check in that direction: distillate stocks built 4.07M bbl on the wire-reported numbers, after the prior week's 3.6M draw took them to 99.3M bbl, the lowest level since May 2003. Even after the build, implied stocks of roughly 103M bbl sit near two-decade lows. The direction has turned; the level has not normalized. That distinction is the whole Q4 debate.

Ranked by sensitivity to that distillate-led rollover:

• VALERO: most direct read-across. Largest Gulf Coast distillate position, the capture leader in Q3, and the closest operating comp to Citgo's Lake Charles and Corpus Christi plants. It gives back the most dollars as diesel cracks fade, and it keeps the most if they stay high. Citgo's ramp in Venezuelan crude purchases also matters here: returning heavy sour barrels widen the heavy discount, and Valero's coking complexity is built to eat exactly that.
• MARATHON: same direction, slightly blunter instrument. Biggest absolute refining system, strong Gulf Coast weight (Garyville, Galveston Bay), so the Q4 step-down applies, but the marketing economics inside its refining and marketing l

The 2025 quarters sum to $453M against the reported full-year $452M (a $1M rounding difference in the company's own tables); the 2026 quarters sum exactly to the reported nine-month figure.

OPERATIONS: THE RECORDS ARE REAL, AND ONE BLOOMBERG WORDING IS IMPRECISE

• Total refinery throughput was 904,000 bpd, up 10 percent on Q2's 820,000 bpd. The crude-only rate was a quarterly record 855,000 bpd, which is 103 percent of rated crude capacity. Bloomberg wrote that the plants "processed nearly 900,000 barrels of crude each day": the 904,000 figure is total throughput including other feedstocks and blendstocks, and it is just over, not nearly, 900,000. The crude figure is 855,000 bpd.
• Distillate production set a combined record of 365,000 bpd, led by a Lake Charles distillate record of 208,000 bpd. Corpus Christi set a quarterly crude rate record of 176,000 bpd. Marketing volume was 411,000 bpd.
• Rated capacity: Citgo's own profile gives Lake Charles 479,000 bpd, Lemont 183,000 bpd, Corpus Christi 167,000 bpd, totaling exactly the 829,000 bpd the release uses (the step-up from 807,000 bpd was documented in the Q3 2025 release). The EIA Refinery Capacity Report (January 1, 2026, calendar-day atmospheric basis) gives 471,200 + 188,023 + 165,000 = 824,223 bpd. The difference is basis and timing, not error; the company's rated figure is the denominator behind the 103 percent.
• Per-refinery throughput for Q3 2026 is not disclosed in the release. A specialist newsletter citing state data puts Corpus Christi at a record roughly 177,000 bpd, Lake Charles around 510,000 bpd through August, and Lemont at about 190,000 bpd. Single source.

posts.text:
$SMCI is the best case study in the market for a hard lesson. A stock can grow as fast as it wants and print amazing fundamentals, and headlines like these will still cap it.

Today, Semafor reports a DOJ probe focused on Supermicro’s connection to Alice Huang, the alleged spy at the center of the Nvidia scandal. The stock is tumbling on it.

And this is not the first rodeo. 

This YEAR alone, a co-founder was arrested for allegedly smuggling $2.5 billion of GPU servers to China, with the DOJ describing dummy servers and swapped serial labels. Before that, the auditor resignation, the delisting scare, the accounting probe, and a 20 year old export violation involving Iran. 

The company was not charged in the smuggling case and says it was a victim, but count the pattern, that is a compliance headline every few months at a company sitting in the middle of the most scrutinized supply chain on earth.

Here is the lesson. The business keeps growing because the AI buildout needs server racks regardless. But the multiple will NEVER get paid what the growth deserves, because every few months the market has to re-price legal risk it cannot model.

Growth builds the valuation, trust builds the multiple, and you cannot compound in a name that keeps making you check the news before breakfast.

There are companies with the same demand exposure and none of the baggage. I own those instead.

Despite all the negative feedback I got for saying on Monday the $NVDA Board would force Jensen Huang out as CEO, Huang resigned this morning and named CFO Collette Kress interim CEO until they find a replacement.  NVDA named veteran board member Harvey Jones (33 years on the $NVDA board) as Chairman. 

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns -- 4th Update

By Robbie Whelan, Josh Dawsey and Amrith Ramkumar 

11/12/2026 08:27:58 [WSJ]
(Wall Street Journal) -- Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang has resigned after two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and another with an employee. 

The company said Thursday that finance chief Colette Kress had agreed to serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is named. The board is starting a search for the company's next CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. 
Nvidia's board also appointed longtime director Harvey C. Jones to become its first ever chair. Jones, a venture investor and technology executive, joined Nvidia's board in 1993, the year the company was founded. 

Kress, who will keep her role as CFO, said as part of the announcement that she is "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." 

Jones added that Kress is supported by an "experienced leadership team" and that the board expects to continue operations and its product roadmap "without interruption." 
Huang's resignation brings down the curtain on an era during which he stoked the global artificial-intelligence boom and became a geopolitical star. It leaves one of the world's most valuable companies in need of a new leader. Huang, a co-founder of Nvidia, is seen by many as the face of the AI arms race. 

Known for his leather jackets and near-constant appearances at conferences and events all around the globe, he spoke with the confidence of a salesman who had just what the world wanted -- and he did. Nvidia's graphics processing units, high powered computer processors packed with billions of transistors, are the central component behind what many believe is the next industrial revolution. 

The chipmaker's importance to global customers made Huang a worldwide celebrity. He frequently met with top U.S. and Chinese officials, and was regularly mobbed by adoring fans when he visited Taiwan, his birthplace and the global manufacturing hub of the chip industry. 

Then, on Sunday, Huang acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized for violating his family's and his employees' trust. That affair involved Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, which has been a major Nvidia customer and who U.S. intelligence officials believe is working for China's intelligence services. 

The Nvidia CEO also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a senior executive at Nvidia who runs the company's healthcare business, according to a person familiar with the matter. The New York Times earlier reported the second affair. Powell didn't respond to requests for comment. 

Shares of Nvidia were down almost 8% in premarket trading Thursday, extending a recent slide following the revelation that Nvidia's board was investigating Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang. The top executive, 63, is Nvidia's largest shareholder, owning about 3.6% of the company, and has become one of the richest people in the world. 

Huang, who had roughly 60 direct reports, has said he doesn't believe in succession planning and that leaders should continuously pass on knowledge and information as they have it. It wasn't immediately clear who would succeed him. 
Nvidia's latest proxy statement warns that it is "highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team" and that the failure to ensure effective succession planning could "hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success."

This hits at a moment of broader AI anxiety: multi-year buildout costs, geopolitical delays on data centers, and the risk that new models reduce the need for expensive inference. All of it has fed the selloff.

None of it changes the underlying reality. We’re still early. Adoption is sub 1%, and the steep part of the inference S-curve is still ahead of us. 

Nvidia’s GPUs remain a step-function better than AMD’s, evidenced by ~
90% GPU market share even at a higher price.

The uncertainty in $NVDA creates a window for new capital to come in and benefit from the next several years of the AI buildout, of which Nvidia will account for about 50% of that cost.

posts.name: Puru Saxena
posts.text:
Jensen Huang’s resignation ends an era at NVIDIA and forces a stress test on the AI trade.

Huang wasn’t just a CEO. He was the face, the product visionary and the operator who turned NVIDIA into the $4T+ foundation of the AI boom. Key-man risk was always priced in at some level; today it is no longer theoretical. $NVDA stock is already down hard (10%+ in premarket) and the rest of the AI complex is feeling the spillover.

The near-term picture is messy. Leadership uncertainty, succession questions and the China-related overhang from the scandal create real noise. Colette Kress (long-time CFO, now interim CEO) and the existing leadership team provide operational continuity and the board has appointed Harvey Jones as its first Chair. Product roadmaps, CUDA lock-in and hyperscaler demand don’t disappear overnight. Still, the narrative premium from $NVDA is gone.

The setup for a multi-week rally is strong. AI stocks were already deeply oversold coming into this news after the recent sharp selloff. Technicals are washed out, sentiment is depressed and multiple strategists had already called the prior dip extreme. Forced selling and panic often exhaust quickly in these regimes. A relief bounce across the AI complex over the next several weeks looks highly probable as the dust settles.

The multi-month view is more nuanced. The AI infrastructure buildout itself is not over. Capex remains massive, data-centre demand is still the dominant growth driver and the underlying technology stack (accelerated computing, inference, networking) continues to expand. What changes is that NVIDIA must now prove it can execute without its founder-CEO narrative. Succession clarity, any regulatory/export fallout and whether the next permanent CEO can maintain the same cultural and technical intensity will decide if this is a healthy reset or the start of a longer period of relative underperformance versus the broader AI complex.

This is a classic “sell the rumor / buy the fact” environment for the trade. Oversold conditions favour a multi-week bounce. The multi-month case for AI stocks rests on whether the structural demand story can remain intact and companies with high margins, FCF and strong balance-sheets are likely to outperform. http://alphatarget.com

📺 A SNAPBACK RALLY IS NOT THE SAME AS A REPAIRED MARKET + $SPY / $QQQ KEY LEVELS  + A DEEP LOOK AT $NVDA + $GOOGL POTENTIAL GAP-FILL TRADE + $TSLA MUST HOLD $386

The market has staged a powerful snapback rally, but that doesn't mean the technical damage has been repaired.

We've seen a sharp rebound that forced shorts to cover, and now comes the real test: can buyers defend these gains, build higher lows, and establish a foundation for a sustainable advance?

*

After a massive selloff that erased the post-midterm gap, broke below $750, and tested the 200-day moving average, $SPY rebounded toward $762.50.

Now I'm watching $755.

Holding that level would be impressive and could allow the market to consolidate constructively.

A retest of $750 and change wouldn't necessarily destroy the setup, but sustained weakness below $750 could bring back choppy, difficult trading conditions.

*

$QQQ has staged a V-shaped recovery from roughly $647 to $695.57.

The question is whether that V can develop into a W-shaped bottom.

The immediate level to watch is $683, where yesterday's low and the 200-day moving average converge.

Holding above that area would demonstrate real commitment from buyers.

A shakeout toward $680 is possible, while a deeper pullback toward $667 could still establish a higher low and set up another advance into Thanksgiving.

*

$NVDA is a great example why you should follow a process instead of blindly buying big stocks.

#Nvidia has fallen sharply from $243, failed its breakout, broken its ascending channel, and remained below key short-term moving averages.

There were warning signs well before the latest controversy surrounding Jensen Huang.

The $164–$165 area is now critical. If #NVDA stays below it, $153 becomes the next potential downside target.

Don't buy a falling knife simply because it's Nvidia!

*

I'm holding a small position in $GOOGL for a potential gap-fill trade.

Despite the damaged chart, #Google could attract some rotation within the Mag Seven.

Ideally, it holds $285 and reclaims $296. A sustained move above $296 could open the door toward $300 or higher.

If the setup fails, I'll respect my stop and move on.

*

#Tesla remains trapped in a frustrating trading range despite its recent four-day recovery.

The key level for $TSLA now is $386. If buyers can defend it and build a base, another continuation setup could emerge.

But I'm skeptical. A failure to hold $386 could lead to a gap fill and another disappointing reversal for #TSLA.

*

Bottom line: if you missed the snapback rally, you haven't necessarily missed the opportunity.

The market needs time to rebuild. I'm watching whether SPY holds $755, $QQQ defends $683, and individual stocks begin reclaiming important moving averages.

Until we see that commitment, staying tactical, managing risk, and waiting for better setups makes more sense than chasing a rally that hasn't yet proven itself.

*

posts.name: Daniel Koss
posts.text:
Why is $NBIS down -15% in pre-market? 🤔

The economics have never looked better.
Pre-tax profitable before the end of 2027.
100% pre-payments.

So why is the stock getting crushed on news that massively de-risks the business long-term?

1) Data center buildout delays
2) In my view, INSANELY low 2027 revenue guidance

First-glance gut reaction:

1) I don't mind the delays. They come from third-party partner projects, not Nebius's own builds, which are all on track. And going forward, 75%+ of projects will be their own.

2) The guidance makes no sense to me at first glance. It doesn't match the capacity they plan to bring online or the $/MW we're currently seeing. I'll study it in detail over the next 48 hours and run the math properly to make sense of it.

The ONLY ways I can explain it:
a) a massive sandbag (like MASSIVE!)
b) they expect very big delays in 2027 (doesn't sound like it from the call)
c) they're selling a huge share of capacity on long-term contracts (3-5 years) at much lower prices than expected -> this seems very possible, to de-risk the business by capping both the upside and the downside.

This was one of the most unusual quarters, in the sense that we got a ton of amazing new insights but also confirmation of very bad delays and low guidance. It's definitely a mixed bag of great and bad stuff. Not the usual pure bull porn.

Considering we went +15% into earnings yesterday, it seems expectations were higher. But let's see what the market thinks over the next few sessions. The Jensen news still seems to be a dark cloud over all AI infra stocks (except $AMD) right now.

Over the next few days, I will go much deeper into all the new info (there's a ton to break down!) and reserve the right to change my mind! I also think there's a very high chance the guidance is just ridiculously conservative.

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Resigns as CEO

NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition

Jensen Huang Resigns
Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO
Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.
Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.
Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.
The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.
NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT.

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE This gets the question exactly backwards. Nobody disputes that Jensen Huang is one of the great entrepreneurs of the age. The question before Nvidia's board is not whether he is great. It is whether he can still be trusted, and in a public company trust is not a sentiment. It is the entire basis on which strangers hand over their capital. It is the foundation of the fiduciary responsibility a CEO accepts when he takes the position.

No one is demanding sainthood. The standard here is far lower, and he failed it. Do not carry on a relationship with a woman US intelligence officials suspect of working for China's Ministry of State Security while your company is the chokepoint of American export controls. Do not violate conduct policies you helped write. Do not tell investors, as a shareholder suit now alleges he did on October 30, that the relationship with Megaspeed was normal, weeks before your own board has to open an investigation. That is not sainthood. That is the floor for running a public company.

Thirty years of building earns gratitude. It does not earn immunity from the rules he set himself. The presumption belongs to founders who comply. He spent his.

The Economist is right that no one is irreplaceable, and its conclusion, that he should go, follows from the same fact. The strongest evidence is his own org chart: dozens of direct reports and no designated successor is not a defense of the man, it is an indictment of the governance he built. A

so tl;dr from 2027 onward we should use a much higher multiple, but on the much lower EV/EBITDA.

posts.text:
Some random thoughts about Jensen.

Jensen met his wife Lori when he was just 17, got married, had kids, and started Nvidia at 30.

He then spent the next 33 years working his ass off building Nvidia into one of the most important companies in the world.

I imagine he probably missed out on a lot of things most young people experience, especially dating and relationships.

I think it’s just human nature. When you’re young and don’t get to experience certain things, you may feel like you’re missing out. And sometimes that feeling stays with you for the rest of your life.

Even when you’re 60, with all the money and success in the world, you may still want to experience what you missed in your 20s.

Maybe that’s part of what happened to Jensen. I don’t know.

I’m not trying to justify what he did. He was incredibly reckless, and it cost him something he spent more than half his life building.

But I also think we sometimes forget that Jensen is just a human being, with desires and weaknesses like the rest of us.

Maybe he spent so much of his life building Nvidia that somewhere along the way, he wanted to experience the life he never really had.

The saddest part for me is how quickly he was pushed out of the very company he built from scratch.

This is a man who literally has the Nvidia logo tattooed on his body, who has called Nvidia his life’s work, working every waking hour, and who dedicated more than half his life to it.

quoted.text:
NVIDIA employees: go on strike. Now.

Not for a raise. Not for more PTO. For your founder.

Jensen Huang was just pushed out in four days, after thirty-three years building the company. The GPU, CUDA, the entire infrastructure the world's AI runs on today. And it ends with a three-line press release on a Thursday morning.

Here are the facts. Sunday, Huang admits to an affair and apologizes to his teams. The board launches an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton and a former federal prosecutor. Thursday, he resigns under pressure. The investigation hasn't reached any conclusion. No technology leak has been established. No misconduct has been announced.

The sentence came before the verdict.

Let me be clear: if the investigation shows that NVIDIA secrets ended up in Beijing, he has to go, and nobody will defend him. But you don't unplug the most important builder of the decade over press reports and a market panic. It's called the presumption of innocence. It applies to founders too.

And it has worked before.

November 2023. OpenAI's board fires Sam Altman on a Friday night. Within days, more than 700 of roughly 770 employees sign a letter: bring Altman back, or we all walk. Five days later, Altman is back, and most of the board that fired him is gone.

Call it the Altman precedent: in a company built on talent, real power doesn't sit with the board. It sits with the people who build.

NVIDIA's engineers hold that power today. They're the ones running the machin

• Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, president and director, effective immediately. CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO; Harvey Jones becomes board chair. This is a massive prospective infrastructure pipeline, not an immediately energized addition to AI computing capacity.

• Applied Materials finished fiscal 2026 with $34.4B in revenue, up 21%, and adjusted EPS of $12.89, up 37%. Semiconductor Systems sales rose 22% to $26.1B; services grew 20% to $6.9B. 🚨 La Chine a entraîné ses meilleurs modèles d'IA sur des puces Nvidia 

C'est ce qu'affirme Will Depue, ex-chercheur d'OpenAI, et sa méthode est assez folle

Quand on crée un modèle d'IA, ses poids partent de valeurs « aléatoires ». Sauf que ce hasard n'en est pas vraiment un : il dépend du GPU exact utilisé. Chaque puce laisse une empreinte, un peu comme une empreinte digitale, et cette trace survit jusque dans le modèle final publié

Il a testé plus de 6 000 milliards de combinaisons sur les modèles open source chinois. 
Le résultat est assez insane : DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3 et MiniMax-M3 portent l'empreinte de Blackwell, la puce la plus avancée de Nvidia, interdite à l'export vers la Chine

Et il l'a vérifié en vrai. Sur un B300, il retrouve à l'identique, bit pour bit, les poids de départ de DeepSeek. Sur un H100, rien ne correspond

Selon son estimation :

> 2 000 à 3 000 GPU Blackwell par modèle
>150 à 200 M$ par cluster
> plus d'un demi-milliard de dollars de puces interdites, rien que pour ces labs

Ce que ça change en vrai : 

1️⃣ Les contrôles à l'export américains fuient, très probablement via des pays tiers ou du cloud loué à l'étranger, c'est la thèse du DoJ sur Alice Huang et Megaspeed
2️⃣ Le récit « DeepSeek fait aussi bien avec moins de compute » prend un sérieux coup (cc les prochina)
3️⃣ La pression monte sur Nvidia et ses revendeurs, en pleine transition après le départ de Jensen et à quelques jours des résultats du 17/11

Il dit que des chercheurs "seniors"  d'OpenAI et d'Anthropic ont vérifié ses résultats. Si ça se confirme, Washington va être furieux

quoted.text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi

posts.name: will depue
posts.text:
I have a major result to share.

I’ve found conclusive forensic evidence that the top 4 Chinese AI labs—DeepSeek, Moonshot, MiniMax and Ant Group—have built their newest models on NVIDIA’s most advanced Blackwell chips, which are barred from export to China.

This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it. When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern—a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model.

Again, this evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking. It’s based on a forensic analysis of the model weights released by the companies themselves.

I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models. In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models—including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3—were initialized on NVIDIA Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in NVIDIA’s flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems.

I then verified these results on real hardware. Running unmodified PyTorch with the seeds I’d recovered, a Blackwell B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s untouched starting weights bit for bit, and a rented GB200 reproduced Kimi K3’s to a correlation of 0.999995. A Hopper H100 reproduced none of DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s, and changing the seed by one broke the match. (DeepSeek’s seed is 953049583 by the way.) The method also was verified to match 24 known open-weights models to the hardware that developers said they used.

It is exceedingly unlikely that these results are a coincidence. Across six trillion combinations, the best accidental match should reach only about 8 sigma (i.e., eight standard deviations above what random chance would produce). The real matches range from 49 to 1,385 sigma, and even the weakest single test hits 20.

These were data-center-scale training runs. With some analysis of release schedules and model details, I estimate that the largest, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, used 2,000 to 3,000 Blackwell GPUs each. Clusters of this size cost on the order of $150 to $200 million each to buy, and across these labs alone would add up to more than half a billion dollars of export-controlled GPUs, not counting experimental compute or otherwise. It’s quite likely that we see multi-billion dollar expenditure on export-controlled GPUs.

I am highly confident in this result, and it has been independently verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic. You can read the full report at http://unemploymentlabs.com/checkpoint-forensics.

There is much more I’ve identified about these models through other forms of checkpoint forensics like this, and will have more to share soon.

posts.name: Downdetector
posts.text:
Microsoft's outage reports on November 12 reached 74 countries and territories in about an hour on Downdetector.

Microsoft says its Exchange Online incident began at 16:17 UTC. Reports to Downdetector about Outlook began climbing at about 17:25 UTC, 12:25 in New York. By 18:25, reports about five Microsoft services combined reached 19,650 a minute, against <15 a minute on an average Thursday. 

Outlook reports alone peaked at more than 2,000 times their normal level.

Reports did not stay in the Americas. They jumped tenfold in the UK at 17:43, in India at 23:21 local time and in New Zealand at 06:55 local time. Between 17:00 and 18:55 UTC, nearly 3 in 10 reports came from outside the US. We count a country here once its reports reach ten times normal and at least 20 in five minutes.

Reports about Microsoft 365, Copilot, Teams and OneDrive each rose more than a hundredfold, and Azure about a hundredfold. Xbox, GitHub and LinkedIn, also Microsoft's, rose far less.

Microsoft said a portion of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load across multiple regions. At 19:38 UTC, reports were still running at more than 11,000 a minute.

Weekly KAOS - The Bullwhip & The Canary

A small wobble in end demand snaps hardest UPSTREAM where the chips, data centers and power sit, and because that upstream now runs on Debt rather than Equity, Credit is the Canary in the Coalmine.

Welcome to the Weekly KAOS — UrbanKaoboy’s end-of-week roundup covering Macro and Geopolitics, where I try and tease out the most impactful bits of the week.

Themes of the Week

The AI trade finally cracked this week, tech tumbled and bonds rallied into the growth scare, which is the Bullwhip snapping upstream and the Credit Canary singing louder.

Anyone who has studied supply chains knows the Bullwhip Effect, where a modest wiggle in end demand gets amplified as it travels upstream, so that a 5% bump at the retailer can balloon into a 40% swing at the factory. As I posted this week, I am not nearly smart enough to know how the AI/Anthropic story ends, but the Bullwhip Effect really concerns me.

Everyone is frothing over that parabolic ARR and forgetting that Anthropic sits near the FRONT of the Bullwhip, while the truly capital-hungry links, the chips, the servers, the gigawatts, sit far UPSTREAM. That is exactly where a small crack at the handle becomes a violent snap at the tip.

posts.name: Patrick Moorhead
posts.text: Will Nvidia's commitment to open-source waver? An Nvidia leader @NaderLikeLadder weighs in on it.

quoted.text:
This is a difficult moment. It’s hard not to look at the journey this company has taken and not be filled with respect for what Jensen built. The spirit of the company remains strong: "mission is the boss”.

That said, as NVIDIA finds its way forward, I want one thing to be clear: NVIDIA's contributions to open source are unwavering.

Jensen has been vocal about this, and that commitment runs deep in NVIDIA's people and culture. We all understand the importance of open source.

NVIDIA is a huge supporter of open source because we understand something.
If you want to diffuse technology, you do so through an ecosystem, not a single company or entity.

No one owns the internet, no one owns servers, and no one owns operating systems… but through open source, an ecosystem of closed and open innovation flourishes.

When we talk about delivering agents safely and securely, that too will take place because of open source. For example, ensuring people have the best models to secure themselves at machine speed unburdened by arbitrary guardrails decided behind closed doors.

Open source & AI are often discussed together, but it’s worth reminding, open source predates AI. It is a mechanism for sharing ideas inspired by the hippies at computer labs of California in the 1960s.

Dylan Patel says Nvidia’s next CEO has to hold off OpenAI, Broadcom, Google, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, and AMD chip teams, who are all 'fucking good'

“It’s not like you’re fighting, no knocks against Palo Alto Networks, but their competitors are not that amazing, versus Nvidia’s fighting an OpenAI chip team, a Broadcom chip team, a Google chip team, an Anthropic chip team, a Meta chip team, Amazon chip team. These guys are fucking good. AMD. They’re all really good, and all these startups.”

“They’re all good. It’s not like they’re incompetent. I think it’s very different. As great as Lisa Su is, she took down Intel, who’s incompetent.”

“What is the person who defined a category and created it and kept all the invaders at bay? It’s very different than being second place or making smart tactical business decisions, innovating on something once there’s already a category established. It’s just very different.”

quoted.text:
Dylan Patel says Nvidia without Jensen Huang becomes a committee that decides slowly, with no clear technical lead and a weaker hand to lock up supply below market rate

“I think that’s the biggest worry for Nvidia, is that now it’s like a committee of people doing stuff. And that’s just gonna make decisions slow. Technically, they could fall behind because of this.”

“There’s sort of three main things. There’s the technical side. Nvidia is so ingrained in helping make decisions there. There’s no one clear technical lead. I mean, maybe Jonah is, but then there’s a lot of people who are also directly reporting to Jensen doing technical stuff, so it’s hard there to move as fast.”

“Supply chain wise, Nvidia wants to do aggressive things, lock up supply, convince the supply chain to do things that they’ve never done before in terms of technology and supply, and locking it up to Nvidia. And that’s probably a lot harder to do given whoever the CEO is is probably not as charismatic as Jensen, and they’re not gonna be like, ‘Yeah, sure, Nvidia. In 2008, a young Ian Buck, now floated as a possible Nvidia CEO, explained how CUDA began: his Stanford PhD project, which Nvidia helped fund and then hired him to commercialize

“My name’s Ian Buck. I’m the director of GPU computing at NVIDIA for software. I received my PhD from Stanford in 2004.”

“Basically, my research at Stanford was looking at general purpose program models for GPUs and trying to understand how we could use these processors for things other than games and graphics.”

“My PhD thesis resulted in a software system called Brook, which was the first attempt at a general purpose programming model and language for GPU computing. NVIDIA was fortunate enough to help fund the work and was very interested.”

“So I finished my thesis in 2004 and came to NVIDIA to take what was a research project to make it turn into a real commercial solution. That’s when we started on CUDA, and for over two years, we were doing internal software development and finally shipped CUDA 1.0 back in 2006 with the GeForce 8800.”

Well-meaning, patriotic China “Hawks” who are not AI/HW experts are putting American national security at risk.

China had *zero* chance of ever catching America in AI with the export strategy that Jensen supported. Given that it looks like the China “Hawks” will get their preferred policy, China will likely soon have a chance of catching America in AI by going down an alternate, less power-efficient AI hardware path. posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Agreed. And it’s a living process. 

Take a $1MM portfolio with a $40K annual withdrawal. The first several years of that need are close to a known quantity. I can match a bond ladder to those withdrawals and I’m barely projecting anything. I call that contractual liability matching. The cash flows are contractual, the liability is near term, and you can discount it mechanically off the TIPS curve. There’s very little guessing involved.

The math gets fuzzier the further out you go. Inflation, spending, and asset returns compound into a wide range of outcomes over 20 or 30 years. That’s where I switch to statistical matching. You’re no longer matching a cash flow to a contract. You’re matching a long duration liability to the asset with the best odds of funding it. If you have a $50K shortfall 30 years out, you likely need a big slug of equities because nothing else has the expected return to cover a liability that far away.

So the plan isn’t one big guess. It’s a small amount of near certainty up front and a growing amount of estimation as you move out in time. The important part is that the near term matching buys you the time to be wrong about the long term stuff. If my 30 year return assumption is off, I find that out gradually and adjust, and the client’s next 5 to 7 years of spending were never at risk while I did. This is what annual reviews are for. 

And the alternative isn’t “no guesses.” Every portfolio embeds a forecast whether you write it down or not. A 60/40 with no plan behind it is still a guess about returns, inflation, and spending. It’s just an unexamined one. I’d rather make the assumptions explicit, match what can be matched, and update the rest as reality shows up.

Good financial planning is a process of making continual guesstimates in a band of probabilistic outcomes.

This is a difficult moment. It’s hard not to look at the journey this company has taken and not be filled with respect for what Jensen built. The spirit of the company remains strong: "mission is the boss”.

That said, as NVIDIA finds its way forward, I want one thing to be clear: NVIDIA's contributions to open source are unwavering.

Jensen has been vocal about this, and that commitment runs deep in NVIDIA's people and culture. We all understand the importance of open source.

NVIDIA is a huge supporter of open source because we understand something.
If you want to diffuse technology, you do so through an ecosystem, not a single company or entity.

No one owns the internet, no one owns servers, and no one owns operating systems… but through open source, an ecosystem of closed and open innovation flourishes.

When we talk about delivering agents safely and securely, that too will take place because of open source. For example, ensuring people have the best models to secure themselves at machine speed unburdened by arbitrary guardrails decided behind closed doors.

Open source & AI are often discussed together, but it’s worth reminding, open source predates AI. It is a mechanism for sharing ideas inspired by the hippies at computer labs of California in the 1960s.

Before AI, the largest shift I lived through was the internet. It was remarkable seeing the fight for open source take place there. Between browsers, runtimes, net neutrality, etc. What came as a result was HTML5 and an extremely vibrant ecosystem that built the internet as we know it today.

NVIDIA and its partners hold an incredibly important role in delivering this technology. NVIDIA contributes to every layer of the stack. Runtimes, models, harnesses, programming languages, frameworks, etc. None of that changes.

Long live open source.

NVIDIA PENALTIES, CONTINUED (2/2)

SECTION 3: SEC AND SECURITIES-LITIGATION CONSEQUENCES

3.1 The class action. Kistenmacher v. NVIDIA, No. 5:26-cv-13448 (N.D. Cal., filed 11/9/26), sections 10(b) and 20(a), class period 10/9/25 to 11/8/26, lead-plaintiff deadline 1/8/27. Challenged statements: the 10/9/25 Rizzo statements (no evidence of diversion; Megaspeed determined not China-owned; site visits found no evidence of diversion); the 10/29/26 Rizzo statement (Huang's interactions with Alice Huang "not unusual or unexpected"); and Huang's 10/30/26 Bloomberg statement (dealings with Megaspeed "normal and not unusual," diversion checked). The falsity theory is that each was misleading because of the undisclosed relationship. Pleaded corrective disclosure: the 11/8 board investigation statement; the stock fell $7.97 (4.27%) to $178.67 on 11/9.

Posture: vulnerable at the motion to dismiss on three grounds. Duty: there is no general duty to disclose a CEO's affair; plaintiffs must tie the relationship to the subject of the statements, export compliance, a half-truth theory that is stronger for the diversion statements than for "normal and not unusual." Scienter: Huang's knowledge of his own relationship is trivially pleaded; knowledge that Alice Huang was an intelligence asset or that diversion occurred is not, and the defense will quote the President's 11/9 account that Huang said he had no idea she was a spy. Loss causation: defendants will argue the drops reflect investigation and scandal news and sector decline, not revelation that the compliance statements were false. If it survives dismissal, settlement benchmarks: the 2025 median securities settlement was $17.3M, mega-settlements of $100M or more averaged about $200M, and Seagate's parallel securities settlement was $175M. On Nvidia's market cap and a year-long class period, a surviving case settles in the high eight to nine figures, ordinarily inside the D&O tower (Side C entity coverage), whose limits are not publicly disclosed. Government fines, by contrast, are generally uninsurable.

3.2 Derivative and books-and-records. Nvidia is Delaware-incorporated, so the vehicle is a section 220 demand followed by a Caremark oversight suit, with export-control compliance as a mission-critical risk, the strongest Caremark category, plus a loyalty claim against Huang. No Huang-specific 220 demand or derivative filing could be verified as of 11/12; treat as expected, not confirmed. The vehicle is already in use against Nvidia over the H200 revenue-share arrangement (the Copus/Paisner Chancery complaint). These matters run two to five years and typically settle for governance reforms and fees; the cash channel is minor unless a personal loyalty claim survives. The first real fight will be the Wachtell report's privilege posture.

3.3 SEC enforcement. The controlling precedent is McDonald's/Easterbrook (January 2023): the SEC charged Easterbrook personally ($400K penalty, five-year officer and director bar) for false and misleading statements about his separation, and charged McDonald's only on proxy disclosure (Item 402) for exercising discretion to treat the exit as without cause, with no company penalty given cooperation. Intel/Krzanich (2018) is the negative precedent: an accurate disclosure, a policy violation, a resignation, and no SEC case. Mapped to Nvidia: SEC risk concentrates on the accuracy of the 8-K and proxy characterization of Huang's exit and its compensation treatment, and on whether the Megaspeed statements entered filings, not on the relationship itself. Realistic range: no action, up to a settled order against Huang personally with a modest penalty and a possible bar, with no or a modest company penalty if the company cooperates. The SEC is a tail risk here, not the main event. Plaintiff-firm "investigation notices" are solicitations, not government action.

posts.text:
All the tech people rushing to defend Jensen are off base.

As a VC, I get it. He's a generational founder, and there's a deeply-ingrained lesson in tech that founders are almost always the best people to run their companies. I share that intuition.

But the board's call here was dead simple:

1. His credibility is shredded. Jensen said two weeks ago that his relationship with Alice Huang was "completely normal and not unusual." Ten days later he admitted the affair. Now there's a second affair, with an exec who reports directly to him. As others have said: "when you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate for the ants in your kitchen is not two." 
2. He violated export controls and tried to quash the investigation into MegaSpeed, which could be an extremely serious crime. The Trump admin is already signaling that they are going to reverse course on export restrictions because of this scandal.
3. The politics has flipped. His relationship with Trump is no longer the asset it was. The Dems are in control of Congress now and there is furious anti-AI backlash that Nvidia will need to weather. Having been compromised by a Chinese spy and advocating for exports to China makes him totally disqualified on these questions going forward. There is going to be hell to pay over the next few years, and Nvidia needs a CEO who can walk into those hearings with legitimacy. Otherwise this cloud would always hang over him.
4. There's a business to run. The dude already wrote one apology letter. Was the board supposed to wait for him to write a second one? A third? You can't run a $4T company like this.

A CEO has to be reliable first and foremost. Once that’s gone, you don’t get it back. 

Jensen will almost certainly have a second act. But just not as CEO of Nvidia.

And anyone calling this a psy-op or a coup should just look at the Polymarket on this. Before the second affair, Jensen was only at 15% to be out as CEO. He could've survived one scandal, and I agreed it'd be foolish to let him go at that point. Easy to argue he was duped and made a mistake.

But you don't get two.

Jensen was probably too naive.

Look at how much voting power these founders have in their own companies:

Elon Musk (SpaceX): 82%+

As all NVIDIA employees I guess, I am deeply concerned by the campaign against Jensen Huang. Removing him would be a disaster.

Many have documented on X and elsewhere how this looks like a coordinated coup.

I'd add only one thing. Look at who would benefit from a dramatic weakening of NVIDIA.

It is not China. It is not about selling GPUs to China because that train has left. China authorities have pushed back on the H200 the Trump administration allowed NVIDIA to sell.

Look at what Jensen pushed back on:
- regulations that would make open source model training too expensive
- regulations that would make closed model providers immune to liabilities caused by their models. He said "if your product is not ready, then don't ship it"
- regulation against model distillation. He said "this is competition. People do it all the time with NVIDIA products, they try to reverse engineer them."

The other side will do everything they can to get him fired. 

As a French, I can't care less about his private life. I get that the US is puritan and sees it otherwise. But frankly, isn't it something he and his family has to deal with? Why should all NVIDIA employees, partners, and investors be collateral damage?

Disclaimer. As my bio says, the above are my views only. I do not represent NVIDIA by any means. I only commented on publicly available information.

Trump says Tim Cook is the best person to take Jensen Huang’s place as Nvidia CEO, but I think where Cook’s strengths would shine most is cost management. Having watched Apple’s supply chain management from the sidelines for more than 10 years, and comparing that with what I’ve learned tracking and researching Nvidia in recent years, I think Nvidia still has clear room for improvement in supply chain and cost management.

As for everything else, especially the most important part, planning and developing new technologies, this isn’t just about Cook. So far, the only CEO who has clearly proven he can do this well, bringing humanity’s most cutting-edge technologies from across fields into AI chips and rack solutions while keeping up a fast pace of commercial iteration, is Jensen Huang. (Of course, others will likely prove they can do this well in the future too.)

Jensen Huang says he loves working with Elon Musk, and reveals their engineering teams are designing a new type of server to put data centers in space

“I’m delighted that I love working with Elon. He’s using our technology for his own AI in training models and such, deploying models, of course."

"Grok Bot is super cool. The demand for Grok Bot, the consumption for Grok Bot is really skyrocketing. And then, of course, he rents it."

"And so the combination of these three things, he’s fairly unique in doing that. I guess Google does that. That would be yet another example."

posts.name: Mark Minervini
posts.text:
The fourth quarter, particularly November and December, is historically one of the strongest periods of the year for stocks. But 2018 is a good reminder that seasonality doesn't always win out, especially when the Fed is tightening and the market is already showing signs of deterioration.

In 2018, the Fed was already raising interest rates when the market started to come under pressure. The S&P 500 broke below its 50-day moving average and sold off hard in October. It then snapped back roughly 8%, which at the time looked like the correction might be running its course, particularly with the market heading into the seasonally strong November-December period.

But the rally failed.

The S&P rolled over and fell another roughly 16% before finally bottoming on Christmas Eve. From the September high to the December low, the decline was nearly 20%.

The point is not that 2018 is going to repeat itself. It's that you can't assume the market is going higher simply because you're entering a historically strong seasonal period. When the Fed is tightening, rates are rising and market conditions are deteriorating, those forces can overwhelm seasonality.

We always respect seasonal tendencies, but we don't trade the calendar. We trade the market in front of us. Price and volume, breadth, leadership, interest rates and, most importantly, the action of individual stocks will tell us whether the market is actually improving.

2018 is a good example of why you have to keep an open mind. Even during one of the strongest seasonal periods of the year, the market can still go down.
