posts.text:
Key takeaways on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation:

1. Near term, the bad news is priced in:
For the stock market, this could be a one-time clearing event. Huang has now fully cut ties with Nvidia, so Congress summoning him and any follow-up investigations should have less impact on Nvidia’s stock from here. As for how Huang’s next moves might affect Nvidia, it’s too early to call before the investigation results are out.

2. Google’s TPU is likely the biggest beneficiary:
With Nvidia facing succession uncertainty, Google’s TPU has a chance to win more trust from customers and the supply chain. Its key partners, MediaTek and Broadcom, could be the market’s near-term focus.

3. Succession impact shows up in 2028 at the earliest:
CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO. The formal CEO transition and the organizational changes that come with it will likely start affecting Nvidia’s product development and competitiveness in 2028 at the earliest.

4. Capacity pre-booking and spec upgrades are the key focus for supply chain checks:
Huang’s product strategy pushed the supply chain hard in two ways: capacity pre-booking and spec upgrades. It’s critical to watch for any changes in capacity expansion and new tech development across the supply chain. These are among the core reasons Nvidia’s supply chain trades at high P/E multiples.

5. China demand and export controls:
The share of Nvidia’s AI chip revenue that ultimately ends up with Chinese buyers may be higher than what the company has officially stated. That’s why some investors worry Nvidia’s revenue will drop sharply once the US government tightens export controls. But China’s end demand won’t disappear because of export controls. Even under tighter rules, as long as overseas resale channels exist, Chinese buyers may still pay the premium, even at several times the price, and get Nvidia chips/racks through indirect routes.

posts.text:
重點分析 Nvidia CEO 黃仁勳辭職：

1. 短期利空出盡：
對股市而言，短期內可能是一次性的利空出盡。黃仁勳目前已與 Nvidia 完全切割，接下來國會傳喚黃仁勳及後續調查，對 Nvidia 股價的影響應該會較小。至於黃仁勳離職後的動向對 Nvidia 的影響，在調查結果出爐前，現在就下判斷仍言之過早。

2. Google TPU 為直觀下的最大受益者：
在 Nvidia 面臨接班不確定性下，Google TPU 可能有機會進一步取得客戶與供應鏈信任，其核心合作廠商聯發科與 Broadcom 或為短期市場焦點。

3. 接班影響最快自 2028 年浮現：
目前 CFO Colette Kress 擔任代理執行長。後續正式 CEO 交接與相應的組織改革，對 Nvidia 產品開發與競爭力的影響，預期最快可能自 2028 年開始浮現。

4. 產能預訂與規格升級為供應鏈研究焦點：
黃仁勳的產品策略對供應鏈有兩大激進影響：「產能預訂」與「規格升級」。未來需密切關注供應鏈在擴產與新技術開發方面有無變化，這是支撐 Nvidia 供應鏈高本益比的核心因素之一。

5. 中國需求與出口管制：
Nvidia 最終流向中國買家的 AI 晶片營收比重，可能高於過去對外的正式聲明。因此，有些投資人擔心，美國政府實施更嚴格的出口管制後，Nvidia 營收將顯著衰退。不過，中國終端需求並不會因出口管制而消失。即使出口管制加嚴，只要海外仍存在轉售管道，即使轉售價格高出數倍，中國買家仍有可能承擔溢價並輾轉取得 Nvidia 晶片／機櫃。

TWELVE HOURS IN THE JENSEN HUANG CASE FROM 10PM TO 10AM on 11/12/26

The case resolved overnight. Nvidia announced this morning that Jensen Huang has resigned, effective immediately, ending the board process that had built through the night: Semafor had reported some directors favored CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, and Kress is the interim appointment in the release. The night also deepened the record behind the case, with the Wall Street Journal's account of the husband who introduced Huang to Alice Huang, Congress turning its fire on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Megaspeed's first public statement, and the analyst downgrade wave broadening before the announcement landed.

HUANG RESIGNS

• Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board of Directors of Nvidia, effective immediately, per Nvidia's own press release issued via GlobeNewswire at 8:48 AM ET today. The release states no reason for the resignation and thanks Huang for his contributions over 33 years.
• Colette Kress, Nvidia's Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer since September 2013, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer while continuing as EVP and CFO until a permanent successor is named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates, per the same release.
• The Board appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board, per the same release. Jones, a director, previously served as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.
• The leadership change does not move the print: Nvidia will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at approximately 1:20 PM PT, followed by its earnings call at 2 PM PT, as previously scheduled, per the same release.

THE BOARD BEFORE THE ANNOUNCEMENT

• Semafor reported last evening, citing people familiar with the matter, that some Nvidia board members favored naming CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO if Huang was removed, ahead of the Wednesday evening board meeting on his future; the full board had not made a decision. That preference is the one the morning release carried out.
• In the same Semafor report, a senior administration official told Semafor that Nvidia's board briefed the White House on its planned Wednesday meeting.
• CNN reported overnight, per two sources, that the board was meeting Wednesday night to discuss Huang's future, and that the same two sources said there was some expectation among Trump administration insiders that Huang would be ousted. CNN reported no decision, vote, or outcome at that time.
• Per the same Semafor report, according to another person familiar with the matter, one person being considered for the permanent top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019.
• Reuters, in a successor canvass published earlier in the window, reported that many analysts and investors saw two people as particularly likely candidates, at least for the short term: Ian Buck, Nvidia's head of product for hyperscale AI, and Kress. In the piece, Josh Gilbert of eToro called Kress the obvious choice to steady the ship while saying the permanent job likely wants an engineer in the chair, and Shay Boloor of Futurum Equities called Buck the strongest long-term internal candidate.

THE HUSBAND

• The Wall Street Journal reported (Lingling Wei) that Huang was introduced to Alice Huang by Chinese businessman Kang Wei, Alice Huang's husband, whom Huang had known for a decade: Kang met Huang in Asia in the 2010s through videogame companies in Kang's investment portfolio, per a person who worked at one of those companies and said he helped connect the two men.

posts.text:
My memo to our clients this morning:

Yesterday, we doubled our already profitable S&P 500 short exposure because we believe the potential for further downside remains worth the miniscule risk we are taking. Our original position has been completely de-risked, and the additional shares were added using what we call an "add and reduce" technique", allowing us to increase exposure without materially increasing overall risk. This puts us in our favorite position: large profit potential with very small risk.

The Nasdaq triggered a follow-through day. We take that seriously, but now we need to see whether the rally can gain traction or if distribution rears its head in the coming days. With a good-sized hedge bet in place, we are open to adding some longs as they meet our criteria. Currently, the list is small, but there are a few names we are considering. Refer to our Focus List for current names.

Many of yesterday's biggest winners were in the AI/technology stocks that had been beaten down and severely oversold. CoreWeave is an especially good illustration. It exploded 24.7% yesterday, but closed at $60.77 versus a 52-week high of $138.2 - still down about 56% below its high. IREN gained 5.6% but closed at $20.84 against a $70.71 high, still roughly 71% below its high. Those are enormous rallies but occurring inside badly damaged charts. Most of yesterday's tech stock rallies occurred within strong downtrends.

Macro and policy risks still argue for staying selective rather than chasing a market with very few sound stock setups. Sticky inflation, the prospect of additional Fed rate hikes, rising long-term interest rates, and increasing talk of regulation surrounding AI and data centers are all reasons to remain cautious about a nascent rally that, so far, has largely been a rebound from an oversold condition.

Interest rates remain particularly important. After pulling back from an overbought condition, the 10-year yield has started turning higher again, while the 1-year yield jumped sharply. That is not exactly the backdrop you want to see if you’re looking for expanding equity valuations and a sustained risk-on move.

Investors Intelligence bulls fell sharply to 37.0% from 42.6% last week, the lowest bullish reading since early April, when bulls reached 33.3%. That's a significant reversal from just six weeks ago, when bulls stood at 57.7% as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were hitting highs. That peak was one of three readings above the 55% danger level that historically signals elevated risk.

At the same time, bears jumped to 24.1% from 18.5%, the highest bearish reading since April. The shift is encouraging from a contrary-sentiment standpoint, particularly after several weeks when bearish readings remained unusually low.

Sentiment is definitely moving in the right direction, but we don't believe the ratio of bulls to bears has reached the extreme normally associated with a major contrary buy signal. For now, we view the change primarily as a directional indication. Optimism is being wrung out and pessimism is building as stocks retreat from their highs. That's constructive, but it isn't necessarily capitulation. We would like to see sentiment deteriorate further before treating it as a powerful contrary signal.

A follow-through day is important piece of evidence, but it is not a license to blindly rush back into the market. The real confirmation will come from the market of stocks - better price action, expanding leadership and a proliferation of quality setups emerging from sound bases.

For now, we are taking a measured approach. We will look to add some long exposure incrementally as individual stocks prove themselves. We strongly advise you only get aggressive on the heels of portfolio traction. The weight of evidence suggests that we are not yet completely out of the woods. Let the market earn your exposure. For now, maintain short (hedge) exposure and adhere to stops.

posts.text:
NVIDIA Announces CEO Transition
November 12, 2026
Jensen Huang Resigns

Colette Kress, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, Appointed Interim CEO

Harvey C. Jones Appointed First-Ever Chair of the Board

SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 12, 2026 NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately.

Colette Kress, current Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA, has agreed to serve as Interim Chief Executive Officer. Kress will continue to serve as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer while serving as Interim Chief Executive Officer until a permanent successor has been named. The Board is initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates.

Kress has served as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NVIDIA since joining the company in September 2013. During her tenure, she has led the company’s finance organization and has played a key role in NVIDIA’s growth and evolution. Prior to joining NVIDIA, Kress spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco and Microsoft.

The Board of Directors appointed Harvey C. Jones as its first-ever Chair of the Board.  Mr. Jones has been an entrepreneur, technology executive, and active venture investor for over 30 years, including serving as Chief Executive Officer and Executive Chairman of Synopsys.

“Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, Chair of the NVIDIA Board of Directors. “She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing NVIDIA’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap. The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”  

“NVIDIA’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Colette Kress, Interim CEO and CFO, NVIDIA. “We will continue advancing the work that has made NVIDIA a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead. Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.” 

Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.

NVIDIA will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 financial results on Tuesday, November 17, at approximately 1:20 p.m. PT, as previously scheduled, followed by its earnings call at 2 p.m. PT.

For anyone who hasn't heard about this yet: ICE showed up at the front door of Dr. Ann Lawani in Lodi, California, while she was still in her pajamas, shackled her at the wrists, waist, and ankles, and shipped her all the way to a detention center in Louisiana.

She’s a frontline nurse who worked through the worst of COVID, directs the master's nursing program at the University of San Francisco (overseeing 230+ nursing students), and takes care of her 83-year-old dad.

When her family and lawyer tried to find out where she was taken, ICE’s online locator came back with "0 results." It turns out ICE quietly changed its policy the day before her arrest to stop listing thousands of detainees in the public database, so her family had no idea where she was for days while she was bounced from Stockton to Bakersfield to El Paso to Louisiana.

DHS put out a statement claiming she had a 2013 removal order, but they conveniently left out that on the *exact same day* in 2013, an immigration judge granted her Withholding of Removal blocking her deportation to Nigeria because she faced persecution there. 

She has zero criminal record, has checked in with ICE for 13 years, and has a valid federal work permit through 2029. Because they legally can't send her to Nigeria, Rep. Josh Harder says ICE has been trying to quietly deport her to an undisclosed third country behind her lawyer's back.

Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

quoted.text:
I think it’s time to revisit the accredited investor laws in the US.

Companies are staying private longer, where only accredited investors (aka rich people!) can invest. Retail investors can only come in after IPO, when much of the upside has already been captured.

These rules were created with the best of intentions, to protect regular people from scams - a noble idea. Unfortunately, in practice they've often made it illegal to get richer, unless you're already rich. A regressive tax!

We have to judge policies based on their outcomes, not on their intentions.

These are two possible routes I see:

1) Replace the rule with something merit-based, like a financial literacy test. Pass it and you're accredited. Having a qualification based on competency rather than your bank balance or income seems far more fair.

2) Remove the rule entirely. Let consenting adults assess their own risk. Disclosure requirements stay and fraud enforcement stays to punish bad actors.

posts.name: Raoul Pal
posts.text:
GDP only grows three ways... more people, more debt or more productivity. 

More people is gone. Demographics were set in stone 30 years ago and nobody can change them. The workforce is shrinking and ageing, so the growth that used to come from simply adding workers has been fading for two decades.

For the last 15 years the gap left by people has been filled with borrowing, more and more of it, until we're now borrowing to pay the interest on the borrowing. That's the debasement everyone feels but cant name. And that lever is spent too.

Which leaves the third one. Productivity. But here's the problem... productivity has always meant people producing more, and we are running out of people. The only way to get a step change in output with fewer workers is machines.

AI and robotics are not a nice to have. They are the one lever still available, and they are the only thing that can get us out of this mess and outgrow the debt rather than inflate it away.

So yes, people are worried about the robots taking their jobs. The alternative is a system with no way out.

What does change is who the value flows to. It goes to whoever owns the networks...

So if the robots are coming for our jobs, then we had bloody well better own the robots.

【翻訳】
　インフレが急上昇するには、潜在GDPを上回るGDPが必要だ。世界のどこでもそれは当てはまらない。米国はよくて潜在水準にとどまっているだけだ。ユーロ圏は産出ギャップが5%、英国は7%、中国は10%だ。このインフレ懸念は単なる原油価格と供給ショックに過ぎない。

【僕の意見】
　それはスタグフレーションの場合、当てはまらないと思う。イラン情勢以降、コア財の上昇率は相対的に低く、たしかにそれは需要の弱さであり、原油価格高騰がインフレをけん引してきた。でも最近は家賃の鈍化が止まったりしてフェーズが変わり始めてる。
　全体の3割を占める家賃の鈍化が止まるのは非常に大きい。これは金利上昇や資材不足で工期の延期中断がおきた影響などで、CPIへの家賃の完全な反映は少しづつ計6か月かかることから最近になり出てきてる。さらにPPIと輸入物価も止まらない👇

✅米国の輸入にとって重要国の直近前年比PPI
ユーロ圏PPI　+11.1%
カナダPPI　+14.5%
中国PPI　+5.7%
メキシコPPI　+5.6%

✅その他先行指標
10月GSCPI　+1.26（プラス圏で上昇圧）

以上を踏まえると、4か月～7か月後まで米国のCPIに潜在的な上昇圧が続くことを示唆してる。もちろんそれは潜在的な圧であり、原油が急落したりすればそれを上回る表面的な鈍化圧はかかる。だけど中間選挙後の今の原油急落ぐらいでは、おそらくCPIには0.4%前後の下押しにしかならない。これだと👆の上昇圧を相殺するのがやっとだと思う。

さらに首席補佐官がスティーブンミラーになったことで、関税などのイベントが警戒されてる。すでにメキシコの追加関税の話が出てきた。

Doing a deeper dive into the blockade, and whether Iran can withstand it, what has struck me so far is that--beyond the fall in Iran's exports of oil and other liquid energy products--the impact on Iran's trade in durable goods is actually a little hard to determine.

-For instance: declared Chinese exports in Sept. 2025 were $420 million; in Sept. 2026, they were $290 million.

-Brazil has not stopped exporting to Iran (chiefly ag products)--$423 million in Oct. 2026, an identical figure as the year before.  

-Turkey exports to Iran have actually *increased* yoy, $400 million in September vs. $263 million the year before.

This is all drawn from available customs data and trade statistics, i.e. formal trade. What is going on informally is harder to track, but is (likely) also continuing despite the blockade and pressure campaign.

Germany Plans to Ready Coal and Oil Power Plants to Save Gas

Germany is preparing to bring back coal- and oil-fired power plants currently held in its grid reserve to the market in case of a natural gas emergency this winter, according to a draft law seen by Bloomberg News.

Coal- and oil-fired units in Germany’s grid reserve are normally kept outside the regular electricity market and activated when needed to stabilize the grid. Under the proposed rules, they would also be kept fueled and ready to replace gas-fired generation if the government declares a gas shortage, freeing up scarce gas for households and industry without permanently returning the plants to the power market. (Bloomberg)

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Trump Doesn’t Need an Iran Deal. The Market Already Made One.

Washington is debating whether President Trump needs a deal with Iran to bring energy prices down. The market has already answered.

Iran’s only real leverage was the threat that Gulf oil couldn’t reach the world. That threat has failed. Saudi Arabia pumped 10.56 million barrels a day in October, up from 6.3 million in April and close to its pre-war high. Riyadh is now fighting for market share, and history shows what follows. The last three times it did, oil fell 57, 60 and 67 percent.

The oil is getting through. Tanker rates west of Suez fell as much as 70 percent in a single week, and the key route from the Gulf of Oman to Asia has roughly halved since mid-October. West Texas crude has dropped from $102 to $87. 

Private capital did the rest. When war-risk premiums hit 10 percent of a ship’s value, Chubb, Beazley and Lloyd’s syndicates moved in to write the business, and competition is pushing premiums back down. Washington’s $40 billion insurance backstop hasn’t written a single policy because it hasn’t needed to. High prices were the cure for high prices.

Isolation is working. Tehran can no longer hold the world’s oil hostage, and a deal now would hand it relief it hasn’t earned. Voters wanted affordability, and the pump is delivering it.

The real threat to that relief is the Federal Reserve hiking rates into an energy shock that is already over. The yield curve is yelling policy mistake!

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
The Dutch, my fellow citizens, are going absolutely berserk over a new tax plan.

Not just because of what's in it, but also because of the extraordinarily amateurish way it has been put together.

The Netherlands has a minority government, meaning governing parties can shop around for parliamentary support to secure a majority.

The tax plan has been changed over and over again, and each time it gets a little crazier.

While its contents are raising plenty of eyebrows, the process of reaching an agreement is becoming downright laughable.

What the Bloomberg snippet doesn't tell you is that the Council of State, the government's most important independent adviser, has strongly argued against it.

The proposal also includes taxing unrealized gains on crypto and precious metals, potentially extending to certain pension-related investments, not shown in the Bloomberg snippet.

And then there's the Dutch Tax Administration, which has already been at the center of a disastrous benefits fraud scandal. It has repeatedly warned that it simply cannot implement the government's ever-changing plans.

So we have a government pushing ahead with a controversial tax plan, its most important adviser raising serious objections, and the tax authority saying it cannot execute it.

Dutch politics is making a complete fool of itself.

European Gas Rises as Cool Weather, Outages Draw Down Stockpiles

European natural gas extended gains for a third day as cold weather in parts of the region contributes to accelerated drawdowns of already thin inventories.

Benchmark futures gained as much as 4.7% on Thursday. As heating demand increases, withdrawals of gas are occurring at a faster pace than at the same time last year, data from Gas Infrastructure Europe show. Meanwhile, unplanned outages in Norway are further tightening supply.

Europe entered this year’s heating season with lower-than-usual stockpiles, after the Middle East war choked off liquefied natural gas flows that previously accounted for a fifth of global exports. Accelerated drawdowns early in the season risk leaving the region more exposed during later winter months, and could also make it harder to replenish the buffer next year. (Bloomberg)

I am in the business of trying to understand the world, and attempting to guess what policy-makers will do next. And, from there, how to position portfolios for it.
When it comes to the narrative below, for me it’s pretty simple:
- Some countries will choose to trade MORE with China. In those countries you CAN buy the bonds.
- Some countries will choose to trade LESS with China. In those countries you can NOT buy the bonds UNLESS they simultaneously embrace large reforms of their welfare state/domestic austerity (which no one is doing right now…).

This is why for the past five years OECD bonds have by and large sucked wind while EM bonds have by and large crushed it. And why this performance divergence will continue.

Again: not putting a value judgement on things, or arguing for one path vs another. I am not a politician or a government adviser (nor do i have any aspirations to be. I love my life as it is). Just highlighting the (what seem to me fairly obvious) financial consequences of policy decisions…
